title: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
summary: Lloyd's algorithm and what inertia really asks for, k-means++ seeding, the honest limits of elbow and silhouette, DBSCAN and HDBSCAN on the same ten points, clustering embeddings, and evaluation with and without labels.
outcomes: Run Lloyd's algorithm by hand: assignments, centroid moves and inertia per iteration, and recognise a local optimum
Explain why inertia prefers convex, similarly sized clusters, and compute k-means++ D squared seeding probabilities
Pick k with an elbow, a silhouette and a normalised criterion, and say what each one cannot tell you
Label core, border and noise points for a given eps and minPts, and explain why one bridge point can merge two clusters
Score a clustering with silhouette, ARI and NMI and avoid the one-cluster, over-splitting and dropped-noise traps

blocks.md:
You have ten incidents from last quarter and no labels. Nobody tagged them with a root cause; you only have numbers you computed from each one. The question is whether they fall into a few recurring patterns, and which incidents belong to the same pattern. That is **clustering**: splitting unlabelled data into groups whose members are more like each other than like the rest.

In the prerequisite course you minimised a loss against known targets. Here there are no targets, so every clustering algorithm has to *define* what a good group is, and different definitions give different answers on the same data. k-means defines it with squared distance to a centre. DBSCAN defines it with density. Neither definition is right in general.

Our ten incidents, two features each. Feature x is how many services logged errors, feature y is how many minutes passed before the first alert fired. Both are already on comparable scales.

- p1 (1,1), p2 (2,1), p3 (1,2), p4 (2,2)
- p5 (6,1), p6 (7,1), p7 (6,2), p8 (7,3)
- p9 (4,2), p10 (4,6)

Real feature vectors are much longer. Ten points in two dimensions are enough to check every number in this course by hand, and every number below was computed from exactly these coordinates.

blocks.title: Ten unlabelled incidents, x to the right and y upward

scenes.caption: The raw data. Two tight groups of four, one point in the gap between them (p9) and one point far above everything (p10).
What most people say by eye: two clusters, plus two points that do not clearly belong to either. Note that k-means has no way to say that.
The best possible k-means answer for k = 2, found by brute force over all 511 two-way splits: inertia 28.8333. p9 and p10 are pulled into the right cluster.
The best k = 3 answer: inertia 10.8. Now p10 gets its own cluster of one, and p9 still sits with the right group.

blocks.md: k-means takes the number of clusters k as input. It represents each cluster by one point, its **centroid**, and it scores a set of centroids by the total squared distance from every data point to its nearest centroid. scikit-learn calls that total the **inertia**; the clustering literature also calls it the within-cluster sum of squares, the sum of squared errors (SSE) or the potential.

blocks.caption: The k-means objective, as stated by Arthur and Vassilvitskii: choose k centres C to minimise the sum over all n points of the squared distance to the closest centre.

blocks.md:
Finding the exact minimum is NP-hard, even for two clusters. The algorithm everyone actually runs is a local search with two steps, usually credited to Stuart Lloyd's 1982 paper on least squares quantisation in PCM:

1. **Assign**: put every point in the cluster of its nearest centroid.
2. **Update**: move every centroid to the mean of the points now assigned to it.

Repeat until the assignments stop changing. Erich Schubert notes that because the least squares objective is so natural, this alternating scheme was probably invented several times independently. scikit-learn still calls it by its name: the default of `KMeans` is `algorithm="lloyd"`.

Inertia is the *entire* definition of a good clustering in k-means. Anything you believe about your clusters that inertia does not measure, such as "this point is an outlier" or "this group is a long thin chain", k-means cannot express.

Three consequences follow from the objective alone, before any algorithm runs.

- **Every cluster is convex.** Points go to the nearest centroid, so the clusters are the cells of a Voronoi diagram of the centroids: one region per centroid, holding the points closest to it. A region like that is convex, meaning the straight line between any two of its points never leaves it. The DBSCAN paper makes exactly this complaint about partitioning methods: "the shape of all clusters found by a partitioning algorithm is convex which is very restrictive".
- **Clusters are assumed to be round and equally spread.** The scikit-learn user guide says k-means "clusters data by trying to separate samples in n groups of equal variance" and that "inertia makes the assumption that clusters are convex and isotropic", so it "responds poorly to elongated clusters, or manifolds with irregular shapes".
- **There is no noise label.** Every point, however weird, is assigned to some cluster and drags that centroid toward itself.

Schubert explains the round-cluster bias precisely: k-means is the limit case of a Gaussian mixture in which all clusters have an identical, spherical shape and assignments are hard. That identical shape is "simply a consequence of the sum of squared errors not including any weights depending on the cluster or axis". There is no per-cluster width in the formula, so there is nothing to make one cluster wide and another narrow.

blocks.prompt: Compare two splits of our ten points. Split D is the one a density method will produce later: {p1 ... p9} together and {p10} alone. Split K is {p1,p2,p3,p4} and {p5 ... p10}. Which has the lower inertia, and by how much?
blocks.reveal:
**Split K, by almost a factor of two.** Computed from the coordinates:

- Split D: centroids (4, 1.6667) and (4, 6). Inertia **56.0**.
- Split K: centroids (1.5, 1.5) and (5.6667, 2.5). Inertia **28.8333**.

So inertia does not merely fail to find the density answer, it actively prefers cutting the nine-point elongated group in half over keeping it whole and isolating the far point. If what you want is "one group plus one outlier", you are asking k-means for something its objective scores as bad.

blocks.question: Your ten incidents really contain one broad recurring failure (eight incidents, spread out) and one tight recurring failure (two incidents, close together). You run k-means with k = 2. What is the most likely outcome?
options: k-means recovers the two groups, because inertia rewards keeping similar points together
k-means splits the broad group in two and merges the tight pair into one of the halves, because that lowers the total squared distance
k-means refuses to converge, because the clusters have different variances
k-means puts the tight pair in their own cluster and marks the broad group as noise
blocks.explain: Inertia has no per-cluster width, so a wide cluster contributes a lot of squared distance. Splitting it buys a big reduction, while separating two nearby points buys almost nothing. This is the "equal variance" assumption in the scikit-learn user guide, and the reason k-means tends to split large clusters and absorb small ones. Noise is not an option: k-means has no noise label.

blocks.question: Which statement about the k-means objective is true before any algorithm is chosen?
options: Inertia is normalised, so a value of 0.3 means a good clustering
Inertia can only be computed if you know the true labels
Clusters are Voronoi cells of the centroids, so each one is convex
Inertia increases with k, which is why you stop adding clusters
blocks.explain: Assignment to the nearest centroid is exactly a Voronoi partition, so k-means clusters are convex; non-convex shapes are out of reach whatever the algorithm. Inertia is not normalised (the user guide: "we just know that lower values are better and zero is optimal"), it needs no labels, and it decreases as k grows.

lessons.title: Lloyd's algorithm by hand, and why the seeds decide

blocks.md:
Let us run the two steps on all ten points with k = 2. The seeds are two data points chosen at random, which is what `init="random"` does in scikit-learn: pick k rows of the data. Say the coin picks p1 (1,1) and p2 (2,1), both inside the left group. Ties in the assignment step may be broken any way you like as long as you are consistent; here a tie goes to cluster A.

The figure shows, for each of the ten points, its distance to centre A, its distance to centre B and the cluster it ends up in. Watch the two centres move and the distances change under them.

blocks.title: Lloyd's algorithm, k = 2, seeded with p1 and p2

scenes.caption: Seeds: centre A = p1 = (1,1), centre B = p2 = (2,1). The two distance rows are computed from those centres; nothing is assigned yet.
Assignment 1: each point takes the smaller of its two distances. Only p1 and p3 are closer to A. Inertia with these centres is 123.0.
Update 1: A moves to the mean of {p1,p3} = (1, 1.5), B moves to the mean of the other eight = (4.75, 2.25). Both distance rows change and inertia drops to 49.5.
Assignment 2: p2 and p4 flip to A, because A is now at (1, 1.5) in the middle of the left group. Inertia with the old centres is 35.25.
Update 2: A = (1.5, 1.5), B = (5.6667, 2.5). Inertia 28.8333, which brute force confirms is the global optimum for k = 2 on this data.
Assignment 3 changes nothing, so the algorithm stops after three assignment steps. p9 is 2.55 from A and 1.74 from B: it joins B without being close to it.

blocks.title: Inertia after every step of that run

scenes.caption: After the first assignment, with the seed centres still in place, inertia is 123.0.
Moving each centre to the mean of its own points cuts inertia to 49.5 without moving a single point between clusters.
Re-assigning p2 and p4 to the nearer centre cuts it to 35.25. Only two points changed hands.
The second centre move reaches 28.8333 and the next assignment changes nothing. Both steps decrease inertia, never increase it.

blocks.md: Why does each step only ever decrease inertia? The assignment step is obvious: every point moves to a centre at least as close as its old one. The update step follows from one identity about the mean, which Arthur and Vassilvitskii quote as a standard result.

blocks.tex: \sum_{x \in S} \lVert x - z \rVert^2 - \sum_{x \in S} \lVert x - c(S) \rVert^2 = |S| \cdot \lVert c(S) - z \rVert^2
blocks.caption: For any set S with mean c(S) and any other point z, the squared error around z exceeds the squared error around the mean by |S| times the squared distance between them. So replacing a centre by the mean of its cluster can only help.

blocks.md:
That also explains termination. Inertia never increases, and no assignment can repeat, so with a finite number of possible assignments the loop must stop. In practice it stops quickly: three assignment steps here, and scikit-learn still caps it at `max_iter=300` with a tolerance `tol=1e-4` on the centre movement.

What the proof does *not* give you is the global optimum. A stopping point is only a local one: no single point wants to move and no centre wants to shift.

blocks.prompt: Rerun the same algorithm with seeds p1 (1,1) and p3 (1,2), the two points stacked on the left edge, instead of p1 and p2. Where does it converge?
blocks.reveal:
**To a horizontal split that no one would draw by hand.** The first assignment sends every point with y = 1 to one centre and every point with y greater than 1 to the other, and that is already a fixed point: centres (4, 1) and (4, 2.8333), inertia **64.8333**.

That is 2.25 times the optimal 28.8333, and nothing in the algorithm notices. Both steps worked perfectly; the seeds decided the answer. Inertia is also the only signal you have, which is the one good news here: 64.8333 next to 28.8333 tells you the run was bad, even without a picture.

blocks.md:
This is not an unlucky corner case. There are 45 ways to pick two distinct data points as seeds here. Running Lloyd to convergence from each one gives:

- 11 of 45 reach the optimum, 28.8333
- 19 of 45 stop at 30.4 or 30.4167 (p9 joins the left group, and at 30.4167 p10 joins it too)
- 5 of 45 stop at 32.0, 5 at 52.875, 2 at 56.0, 3 at 64.8333

So 34 of 45 random seedings, about 76 percent, end somewhere worse than the optimum, and the worst is 2.25 times worse. With ten points. Arthur and Vassilvitskii note that the ratio of the result to the optimum can be unbounded even with random seeding, and not because of adversarial inputs.

**k-means++** fixes the seeding rather than the loop. Pick the first centre uniformly at random from the data. Then pick each remaining centre at random too, but with probability proportional to the squared distance from that point to the nearest centre already chosen. Write $D(x)$ for that distance; the paper calls this "$D^2$ weighting".

blocks.tex: \Pr[\text{next centre} = x] = \frac{D(x)^2}{\sum_{x' \in X} D(x')^2}, \qquad D(x) = \min_{c \in C} \lVert x - c \rVert
blocks.caption: k-means++ seeding: far-away points are far more likely to be picked, but it is still random, so an outlier cannot force the result the way a deterministic farthest-point rule would.

blocks.title: Probability of each point as the second seed, given p1

scenes.caption: Uniform seeding: every point other than p1 has probability 1/9, about 11.1 percent. One third of the time the second seed lands inside the left group, where p1 already is.
D squared weighting, with the sum of squared distances to p1 equal to 175: p2 and p3 drop to 0.57 percent each, p4 to 1.14, while p8 rises to 22.86 and p6 to 20.57.

blocks.md:
Totalled up: the chance that the second seed lands inside the left group with p1 falls from 33.3 percent to **2.3 percent**, and the chance it lands in the right group rises from 44.4 percent to **72.6 percent**. The bad seedings from the previous figure are exactly the ones this makes unlikely.

One honest caveat from the same bars: p10, the far outlier, gets 19.4 percent. D squared weighting is biased toward outliers, which is why it samples rather than always taking the farthest point, and why you still run several seedings and keep the lowest inertia.

k-means++ is the only step here with a guarantee. Arthur and Vassilvitskii prove $E[\phi] \le 8(\ln k + 2)\,\phi_{OPT}$ after seeding alone, before a single Lloyd iteration; the iterations can then only lower it. In scikit-learn `init="k-means++"` is the default (a greedy variant that tries several candidates per step), and `n_init="auto"` means 1 run with k-means++ but 10 runs with `init="random"`.

blocks.question: You run KMeans twice on the same data with the same k and get inertia 41.2 and 38.7. What should you conclude?
options: The run with 38.7 is the better local optimum of the same objective, and you should keep it
The data has no cluster structure, since the answer is not stable
Inertia is not comparable between runs, so neither number means anything
k is too large, because a correct k always converges to the same inertia
blocks.explain: Different seeds reach different local optima of one fixed objective, and inertia is directly comparable between runs on the same data with the same k. That is why scikit-learn runs the algorithm n_init times and keeps the best inertia. Instability says something about the seeding, not about whether structure exists.

blocks.question: Which seeding rule does k-means++ use for the centres after the first?
options: The point farthest from all chosen centres, deterministically
The point with the highest local density that is not yet a centre
A point sampled with probability proportional to its squared distance to the nearest chosen centre
A point sampled uniformly from the cluster with the largest current inertia
blocks.explain: D squared weighting samples; it does not take the maximum. Sampling is what keeps a single far outlier from being chosen every time, and it is what the O(log k) proof needs. Always taking the farthest point is a different algorithm (farthest-first traversal) with different failure modes.

lessons.title: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits

blocks.md:
k is an input, so you have to pick it. The obvious idea is to run k-means for several k and look at the inertia. Brute force over all partitions of our ten points gives the exact optimum for each k:

- k = 1: SSE 72.9
- k = 2: SSE 28.8333
- k = 3: SSE 10.8
- k = 4: SSE 5.75
- k = 5: SSE 3.3333

It only ever goes down, and that is not a property of this data. Given any solution for k, Schubert points out you can trivially build a better one for k + 1 by making a point with non-zero error into its own centre. So "lowest SSE" always answers k = n.

The **elbow method** therefore looks for the k where the curve stops dropping steeply, on the theory of diminishing returns: before the elbow you are separating real clusters, after it you are cutting real clusters in half.

The figure plots our five SSE values against a baseline. If you slice a one-dimensional uniform interval into k equal pieces, the total variance falls as $1/k$, so Schubert suggests comparing the measured SSE against the naive estimate $\mathrm{SSE}_1 / k$, which here is $72.9/k$. Anything that merely tracks the baseline is not finding structure, it is just quantising.

blocks.title: Inertia against k, with the SSE1/k baseline

scenes.caption: The five exact optima. There is a bend near k = 2 to 3, but no sharp corner: the drop from 2 to 3 is 18.0 and from 3 to 4 is 5.05.

The grey curve is what pure quantisation of structureless data would roughly give. Our points sit below it from k = 2 on, and the biggest step below it comes at k = 3, which is the signal that real groups are being separated.
Ratios SSE_k divided by 72.9/k: 1.000, 0.791, 0.444, 0.316, 0.229. The big gain is at k = 3 and the curve keeps improving after it, so even normalised there is no single obvious answer.

blocks.md: The elbow is not a quantity, it is a shape in a picture. Schubert's objections: the two axes have different meanings, so an "angle" or "slope" has no units; scaling your data by a factor a multiplies SSE by a squared and moves the apparent elbow; and changing the range of k you plot moves it again. The table in the paper shows every published elbow detector failing both on data with many clusters and on uniform noise.

Criteria that compare with a baseline do better. The oldest is the **variance ratio criterion** of Calinski and Harabasz, which divides the variance explained per extra cluster by the variance left per remaining degree of freedom. It is the one scikit-learn exposes as the Calinski-Harabasz score.

blocks.caption: On our ten points: VRC is 12.23 at k = 2, 20.13 at k = 3, 23.36 at k = 4 and 26.09 at k = 5. It keeps rising, so on this tiny data set it would happily take k = 5.

blocks.md: The other standard answer is the **silhouette**, introduced by Rousseeuw in 1987. It scores each point separately. Let $a(i)$ be the mean distance from point i to the other points in its own cluster, and $b(i)$ the mean distance to the points of the nearest other cluster.

blocks.caption: Near 1 means the point is much closer to its own cluster than to the next one; near 0 means it is on the boundary; negative means it is on average closer to another cluster than to its own.

blocks.md:
Worked on the optimal k = 2 split, {p1,p2,p3,p4} and {p5 ... p10}.

For p1: distances to p2, p3, p4 are 1.00, 1.00, 1.41, so $a = 1.1381$. Distances to the six points of the other cluster are 5.00, 6.00, 5.10, 6.32, 3.16, 5.83, so $b = 5.2361$ and $s = 0.7827$.

For p9: it is in the right cluster, so $a$ is its mean distance to p5, p6, p7, p8, p10, which is $(2.236 + 3.162 + 2.000 + 3.162 + 4.000)/5 = 2.9121$. Its mean distance to the left cluster is $(3.162 + 2.236 + 3.000 + 2.000)/4 = 2.5996$. So $s(9) = (2.5996 - 2.9121)/2.9121 = -0.1073$: **negative**, correctly flagging that p9 is in the wrong cluster for its geometry. p10 scores 0.0746, just as unconvincing.

blocks.title: Mean silhouette of the optimal partition, per k

scenes.caption: k = 2 averages 0.5075. The four left points score 0.72 to 0.78, the right group 0.48 to 0.55, and p9 and p10 drag the mean down.
k = 3 averages 0.5438, the best of the four. Pulling p10 out of the big cluster cuts the mean within-cluster distance for the points left in it, so p5, p6 and p7 climb from about 0.5 to about 0.65.
k = 4 drops to 0.3852 and k = 5 to 0.3278: splitting the real groups hurts. Unlike SSE and VRC, silhouette has a maximum you can point at, here k = 3.

blocks.md: Three things the silhouette cannot do. It is undefined for k = 1, so it can never tell you "this data has no clusters" (our k = 3 winner at 0.54 is not strong evidence of anything). It needs all pairwise distances, so it costs O(n squared) work. And it rewards compact well-separated blobs, so it is biased toward the kind of answer k-means produces, which makes it a poor referee between k-means and a density method.

Three criteria, three answers on the same ten points: the elbow is ambiguous, VRC says k = 5, silhouette says k = 3. That disagreement is the lesson. Schubert's advice is to use a baseline-aware criterion (VRC, BIC or the gap statistic) rather than an elbow, and to spend your effort on preprocessing, "because garbage in, garbage out".

blocks.question: A colleague plots inertia for k = 2 to 10, sees the steepest bend at k = 4, and says the data has four clusters. What is the strongest objection?
options: Inertia should go up with k, so their plot must be wrong
The elbow depends on the axis scaling and on the range of k plotted, and the same shape appears even for uniform data with no clusters
They should have used inertia divided by n, which would move the elbow to the right
Four clusters cannot be checked without ground truth labels
blocks.explain: Schubert's point: the curve looks the same on well separated blobs, on 25 blobs and on uniform noise, so a bend is not evidence of structure. Rescaling the data multiplies SSE by a squared and moves the apparent elbow, and starting the plot at k = 2 instead of k = 1 changes it again. Inertia does decrease with k, and dividing by n changes nothing about the shape.

blocks.question: A clustering gives point q a silhouette of -0.35. What does that say?
options: q is an outlier that belongs to no cluster
The clustering has too few clusters, since silhouettes cannot be negative otherwise
q is exactly on the boundary between two clusters
q is on average closer to the points of another cluster than to the points of its own
blocks.explain: Negative means b(i) is less than a(i): the mean distance to the nearest other cluster is smaller than the mean distance to its own cluster members. A value near 0, not negative, means a boundary point. The silhouette has no notion of noise, and negative values can appear at any k.

lessons.title: DBSCAN: core points, border points and noise

blocks.md: k-means had to swallow p9 and p10, and we saw that its objective actively prefers cutting the elongated group of nine over isolating the far point. **DBSCAN**, published in 1996 by Martin Ester, Hans-Peter Kriegel, Joerg Sander and Xiaowei Xu, starts from a different idea: a cluster is a region where points are packed densely, and "the density within the areas of noise is lower than the density in any of the clusters". It takes no k. It takes two parameters, a radius and a count.

blocks.tex: N_{\varepsilon}(p) = \{\, q \in D : d(p,q) \le \varepsilon \,\}, \qquad p \ \text{is a core point} \iff |N_{\varepsilon}(p)| \ge \text{minPts}
blocks.caption: The eps-neighbourhood and the core point condition. The neighbourhood contains p itself, so minPts counts the point: the scikit-learn min_samples doc says "This includes the point itself", and the paper's pseudocode marks a point as noise when its own region query returns fewer than MinPts points.

blocks.title: All pairwise distances, and what eps selects

scenes.caption: Euclidean distances between all ten points, rounded to two decimals. DBSCAN never looks at anything else.
Highlighted: the 20 ordered pairs within eps = 1.5. Row p9 and row p10 are empty, so with minPts = 3 neither can be core, and neither sits inside anyone else's neighbourhood.
Row p9 alone. Its two nearest neighbours, p4 and p7, are both at exactly 2.00, one in each group. Everything about this data set hinges on whether eps reaches 2.00.
At eps = 2.0 there are 26 pairs. p9 gains p4 and p7, and p8 gains p6, taking p8 from 2 neighbours to 3. Those three new links change the answer completely.

blocks.title: Neighbourhood size, role and cluster, for four parameter settings

scenes.caption: eps = 1.0, minPts = 3. Counts include the point itself. p8, p9 and p10 are noise, and the right group is a three-point cluster with p5 as its only core point.
eps = 1.5, minPts = 3. p8 is now within 1.41 of the core point p7, so it joins as a border point. Two clean clusters of four, with p9 and p10 as noise. This is the answer we wanted.
eps = 2.0, minPts = 3. p9 now has three neighbours including itself, so it becomes a core point, and a core point in the gap glues the two groups into one cluster of nine.

eps = 2.0, minPts = 4. p9 has 3 neighbours, below 4, so it is only a border point and the two clusters separate again. It is within eps of core points in both, so it joins whichever cluster is found first.

blocks.md:
The last scene is the one wrinkle in DBSCAN's determinism. The paper is explicit: if a border point falls in the neighbourhood of core points from two different clusters, "point p will be assigned to the cluster discovered first", and apart from that rare case the result is independent of the visiting order.

The chain below is the eps = 2.0, minPts = 3 case written out as the paper's definitions: a sequence of directly density-reachable steps, each one standing on a core point, ending at p8, which is only a border point at eps = 1.5 but becomes core once eps reaches 2.0.

scenes.caption: Start from the core point p1. Every edge drawn here is at most eps = 2.0, so each endpoint is in the other's neighbourhood.
p4 is in p1's neighbourhood and p1 is core, so p4 is directly density-reachable from p1.
p9 is directly density-reachable from p4. This is the step that does not exist at eps = 1.5, where the nearest neighbour of p9 is 2.00 away.
p9 is itself core at eps = 2.0, so the chain continues through it to p7 in the right group. p7 is now density-reachable from p1, which makes them one cluster.
p8 is in p7's neighbourhood but has only 3 neighbours of its own at eps 2.0 with minPts 3, so it is core here too. At eps = 1.5 it was a border point: reachable from p7, reaching nobody.

blocks.prompt: You are happy with eps = 1.5, minPts = 3: two clusters of four and two noise points. An ingestion bug then writes two extra copies of incident p9, both at exactly (4,2), and you rerun with the same parameters. What changes?
blocks.reveal:
**A third cluster appears out of what was noise.** Each of the three copies at (4,2) now has a neighbourhood of 3 (itself and the two others, all at distance 0.00), which meets minPts, so all three are core points and they form a cluster.

They still do not merge the two real groups: p4 and p7 are 2.00 away, beyond eps = 1.5. But raise eps to 2.0 and that same pile in the gap glues everything together.

Density counts cannot tell a repeated event from a dense region, so duplicates are the most common reason a density clustering changes overnight. scikit-learn suggests exactly this fix: remove near-duplicate points and pass their multiplicity as `sample_weight`.

blocks.md: eps is the parameter that decides everything, and it is not scale free. The scikit-learn doc calls it "the most important DBSCAN parameter to choose appropriately for your data set and distance function" and says it "usually cannot be left at the default value": too small and almost everything is labelled -1, too large and separate clusters merge. A single point, p9, moved us from two clusters to one by a change of 0.5 in eps.

The paper's own heuristic for eps is the **sorted k-dist graph**: for each point take the distance to its k-th nearest neighbour, sort those values descending, and look for the first valley, because "all points with a higher k-dist value, left of the threshold, are considered to be noise". The authors fix k = 4 for two-dimensional data, since the graphs for larger k "do not significantly differ from the 4-dist graph".

With minPts = 3, our 3-dist values sorted descending are 4.47 (p10), then 2.24, 2.24, 2.24, 2.00, then 1.41 five times. The drop from 2.24 to 1.41 is the valley, which puts eps somewhere in 1.4 to 2.2, exactly the range in which the answer flips. Ten points is too few for the heuristic to be decisive, and that is worth seeing: it narrows the choice, it does not make it.

blocks.question: With eps = 1.5 and minPts = 3, point p8 has exactly 2 points within eps (itself and p7). Why is p8 still part of a cluster?
options: Because 2 is at least minPts minus 1, which is the real core condition
Because it is a border point: it is inside the eps-neighbourhood of the core point p7
Because DBSCAN assigns every non-noise point to the nearest cluster centroid
Because minPts is only applied to the first point visited in each cluster
blocks.explain: p8 is not core (2 is less than 3), but it is directly density-reachable from p7, which is core, so it joins p7's cluster as a border point. DBSCAN has no centroids, and the core condition applies to every point.

blocks.question: Which of these can DBSCAN do that k-means cannot, on the same data?
options: Guarantee the globally optimal clustering for its objective
Run without computing any distances
Return a chain-shaped cluster and label a far-away point as belonging to no cluster
Produce exactly the number of clusters you ask for
blocks.explain: Density connectivity can follow an arbitrary shape and leaves points outside every cluster as noise (label -1). k-means clusters are convex Voronoi cells and every point is assigned. The number of clusters is an output of DBSCAN, not an input, and both methods are distance-based.

lessons.title: HDBSCAN: a hierarchy instead of one eps

blocks.md: One global eps assumes every cluster has the same density. Our two groups are not equally dense: counting three neighbours, the third-nearest is 1.00 away everywhere in the left group but 1.41 away for p6 and p7 and 2.00 for p8. That is already enough that eps = 1.0 left p8 outside while eps = 2.0 merged everything. **HDBSCAN**, by Ricardo Campello, Davoud Moulavi and Joerg Sander, removes the choice: it runs the density idea at every eps at once and then keeps the clusters that persist. The scikit-learn docs describe it as performing "DBSCAN over varying epsilon values" and integrating the result "to find a clustering that gives the best stability over epsilon".

blocks.caption: Mutual reachability distance, where core_k(x) is the distance from x to its k-th nearest neighbour counting itself. Dense points keep their true distance; sparse points get pushed away from everything by at least their own core distance.

blocks.md:
With k = 3 (`min_samples=3`), the core distances of our points are 1.00 for p1 to p5, 1.41 for p6 and p7, 2.00 for p8 and p9, and 4.24 for p10. Build the minimum spanning tree of the mutual reachability distances and its nine edge weights come out as 1.00, 1.00, 1.00, 1.41, 1.41, 2.00, 2.00, 2.00 and 4.24.

Adding those edges in increasing order is single-linkage clustering: each edge merges the two groups it joins, and the record of those merges is a dendrogram, a tree whose height is the distance at which each merge happened. Cutting it at a distance recovers the DBSCAN result for that eps, or almost: the scikit-learn `dbscan_clustering` method notes this gives DBSCAN*, "DBSCAN without the border points". So the one tree holds every eps at once. HDBSCAN then converts distance to a density scale, $\lambda = 1/\text{distance}$, and condenses the tree: at each split, a branch with fewer than `min_cluster_size` points is not a new cluster, its points simply fall out of the parent at that lambda.

scenes.caption: At lambda 0 (infinite distance) everything is one cluster. Increasing lambda means raising the density threshold, which breaks pieces off.
The last MST edge has weight 4.24, so at lambda = 1/4.24 = 0.236 p10 separates. One point is fewer than min_cluster_size, so it is not a new cluster: it falls out as noise.
At lambda = 1/2.0 = 0.5 the remaining nine split into a group of five and a group of four. Both are at least min_cluster_size, so this is a real split and two child clusters are born.
Stability, the sum of (lambda_p minus lambda_birth) over members: 2.00 on the left, 0.62 on the right. The left cluster survives to lambda 1.0, the right only to 0.707, which is why it scores lower.

blocks.caption: Cluster stability. lambda_p is the density level at which point p drops out of C. A cluster that holds all its members over a wide band of densities scores high; one that shatters immediately scores low.

blocks.md:
The numbers for our ten points, with min_cluster_size = 3:

- Left child {p1,p2,p3,p4,p9}: born at 0.5, p9 drops out immediately at 0.5 and so adds nothing, the other four survive until lambda 1.0. Stability $4 \times 0.5 = 2.00$.
- Right child {p5,p6,p7,p8}: born at 0.5, p8 drops out at 0.5, the other three survive to lambda 0.7071. Stability $3 \times 0.2071 = 0.62$.
- The root, counting p10 leaving at 0.236 and the nine others at the 0.5 split: 4.74.

Extraction walks up the condensed tree, selecting a parent only when its stability beats the sum of its children's. Here the two children sum to 2.62 against the root's 4.74, so the rule alone would take the root, which is precisely why `allow_single_cluster` defaults to False: "by default HDBSCAN will not produce a single cluster". With the root excluded, the answer is the two children, with p10 as noise, and p9 the weakest member of the left cluster.

HDBSCAN trades eps for min_cluster_size, which is usually easier to set because it is a statement about how big a group has to be to matter. In scikit-learn, `min_cluster_size` defaults to 5, `min_samples` defaults to min_cluster_size, and the default `cluster_selection_method="eom"` is the excess-of-mass rule above; `"leaf"` instead keeps the finest clusters at the leaves.

blocks.question: Mutual reachability distance replaces d(a,b) by max of the two core distances and d(a,b). What does that buy?
options: It pushes points that live in sparse regions away from everything, so a lone point cannot act as a bridge between two dense groups
It makes the distance matrix sparse, so the MST is cheaper to build
It normalises all distances to the range 0 to 1, which makes lambda well defined
It makes the clustering independent of min_samples
blocks.explain: A point in a sparse region has a large core distance, so every mutual reachability distance involving it is at least that large. That is exactly the p9 problem from the DBSCAN lesson, handled structurally: p9 has core distance 2.00, so it cannot join either group any earlier than lambda 0.5. The transform depends on min_samples through the core distance, and it does not sparsify or normalise anything.

lessons.title: Clustering embeddings of logs and incidents

blocks.md:
A very common reason to cluster in practice is text: a million log lines, three months of alert descriptions, a backlog of support tickets. You turn each one into an **embedding**, a fixed-length vector from a model or from TF-IDF, and cluster the vectors. The grouping then depends on how you measure similarity between them, and that choice is as important as the algorithm.

For text, similarity almost always means **cosine**: the angle between the vectors, which ignores their length. Length usually encodes something you do not want to cluster on, such as how long the message is or how often that template fired.

blocks.tex: \lVert u - v \rVert^2 = \lVert u \rVert^2 + \lVert v \rVert^2 - 2\, u \cdot v = 2 - 2\cos\theta \quad \text{when} \ \lVert u \rVert = \lVert v \rVert = 1
blocks.caption: The key identity: on vectors of unit length, squared Euclidean distance is a strictly increasing function of the angle. Rank by one and you have ranked by the other.

blocks.title: Distance between unit vectors as a function of angle

scenes.caption: Both curves rise monotonically from 0 at angle 0 to their maximum at 180 degrees, so on normalised vectors Euclidean k-means and cosine similarity agree on every ranking.
At 45 degrees the squared distance is 2 - 2(0.7071) = 0.5858 and the distance is 0.7654. At 90 degrees they are 2 and 1.4142. This holds only after normalisation.

blocks.md:
Here is what skipping the normalisation costs. Five toy vectors stand in for five log templates; two dimensions keep the arithmetic checkable, but a real embedding would have hundreds.

- e1 = (4, 0), length 4.00, angle 0 degrees
- e2 = (1, 0), length 1.00, angle 0 degrees
- e3 = (1, 1), length 1.41, angle 45 degrees
- e4 = (0, 3), length 3.00, angle 90 degrees
- e5 = (0.5, 2), length 2.06, angle 76 degrees

e1 and e2 are the *same* message, one from a chatty service and one from a quiet one. Cosine says they are identical. Raw Euclidean says they are 3.00 apart, further than e2 is from e3 (1.00), a different message.

blocks.title: Cosine, raw Euclidean and unit Euclidean on five vectors

scenes.caption: Cosine similarity. e1 and e2 are a perfect 1.0, e1 and e4 are orthogonal at 0.0, and the nearest pair after e1 and e2 is e4 with e5 at 0.97.
Raw Euclidean distance on the same vectors. Now e1 and e2 are 3.00 apart, the largest value in e2's row apart from e4, and e2's nearest neighbour is e3 at 1.00. Length has taken over.
Euclidean distance after dividing each vector by its length. e1 to e2 is 0.00, e3 to e5 is 0.5339 and e4 to e5 is 0.2444: the same ordering as cosine, because distance is now sqrt(2 - 2 cos).

blocks.md:
Run k-means with k = 2 on these five vectors, exactly optimally, and the normalisation changes the answer:

- raw vectors: {e1} and {e2, e3, e4, e5}, inertia 5.6875. The chatty copy of a message gets a cluster of its own, because it is simply the longest vector.
- unit vectors: {e1, e2} and {e3, e4, e5}, inertia 0.3102. The duplicate message is reunited and the split is now by angle: the two vectors at 0 degrees on one side, the three between 45 and 90 degrees on the other.

The scikit-learn text clustering example is blunt about this: word count vectors "are then normalized to each have l2-norm equal to one (projected to the euclidean unit-sphere) which seems to be important for k-means to work in high dimensional space".

blocks.caption: Expanding the assignment step: the length of x cancels, but the lengths of the centroids do not. A mean of unit vectors is shorter than 1, and by different amounts per cluster, which is why spherical k-means renormalises the centroids after each update so that the comparison really is by cosine.

blocks.md: Two more traps on embeddings. First, dimensionality: the user guide warns that "in very high-dimensional spaces, Euclidean distances tend to become inflated" and suggests reducing dimension (for text, a truncated SVD, which is latent semantic analysis) before k-means; the example re-normalises after the SVD, "since SVD results are not normalized". Second, duplicates: a thousand copies of one log line form a dense cluster all on their own, so deduplicate templates or carry counts as weights.

A practical recipe for grouping incidents or log templates: extract templates, deduplicate, embed, L2 normalise, reduce dimension if the vectors are sparse, then cluster. Use HDBSCAN when you expect a long tail of one-off messages that should be noise, and k-means when you need a fixed number of buckets, for example one dashboard row per group.

blocks.question: You cluster L2-normalised sentence embeddings with KMeans using Euclidean distance. A reviewer says you should have used cosine. What is the accurate reply?
options: They are right: Euclidean distance and cosine similarity disagree on normalised vectors
On unit vectors squared Euclidean distance is 2 - 2 cos, so the assignment step ranks candidates identically; the only wrinkle is that updated centroids are no longer unit length
It makes no difference either way, since k-means ignores the metric and only uses means
Cosine cannot be used with k-means at all, because cosine is a similarity and not a distance
blocks.explain: The identity makes the two orderings the same for unit-length points against a fixed centroid. What breaks the exact equivalence is the centroid: a mean of unit vectors has norm below 1, and the assignment compares x dot c minus half the squared norm of c, so centroid norms matter. Spherical k-means renormalises the centroids to remove that difference.

blocks.question: Raw TF-IDF vectors of log lines are clustered with k-means and one cluster contains only the single longest message, while everything else is in one huge cluster. What is the first thing to fix?
options: Increase k until the huge cluster breaks apart
Switch from k-means to DBSCAN with the default eps
L2 normalise the vectors so that message length stops dominating the geometry
Lower n_init to 1 so the run is faster and more stable
blocks.explain: That failure is the e1 case: an unnormalised vector with a large norm sits far from the origin and from everything else, so it earns its own centroid. Normalisation projects everything onto the unit sphere and leaves only direction. Raising k or switching algorithm without fixing the representation keeps the same bad geometry, and DBSCAN's default eps of 0.5 is meaningless for an unknown scale.

lessons.title: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels

blocks.md:
There are two situations, and they call for different metrics.

**No labels.** You only have the data and the clusters, so all you can measure is geometry: are the clusters compact and separated? The silhouette from lesson 3 is the standard choice, with Calinski-Harabasz and Davies-Bouldin as alternatives. These are the numbers you can compute in production, and they are all biased toward some shape.

**Labels for part of the data.** Someone has read the postmortems and tagged a sample with its real cause. Now you can compare two partitions of the same points, which is what the adjusted Rand index and normalised mutual information do.

Start with the label-free trap. Two results on our ten incidents:

- k-means with k = 2 scores a mean silhouette of 0.5075 over all ten points.
- DBSCAN with eps = 1.5 scores 0.7392, but only over the eight points it put in clusters; its two noise points have no silhouette at all.

0.7392 is not better than 0.5075, it is a different question. Comparing them would reward any method that quietly declares the hard points to be noise. The scikit-learn example makes a related warning about comparing across representations: "strictly speaking, one should not compare the Silhouette Coefficient between spaces of different dimension". Always report the coverage alongside the score: 8 of 10 points clustered.

Now suppose someone reads all ten postmortems and finds three real causes:

- cause 1: p1, p2, p3, p4 and p9 (five incidents, a slow dependency)
- cause 2: p5, p6, p7, p8 (four incidents, a bad deploy)
- cause 3: p10 (one incident, unique)

Note that the truth disagrees with the geometry: p9 belongs with the left group even though it sits in the gap. Ground truth usually does disagree, which is the whole reason to measure. The table below is a contingency table: cell (i, j) counts the points whose true cause is i and whose predicted cluster is j. It crosses the truth against four candidate clusterings, and a predicted label of -1 means noise.

blocks.title: Contingency tables: true cause against predicted cluster

scenes.caption: k-means k = 2 at its global optimum, inertia 28.8333. C1 is a bag of three different causes: four from cause 2, plus p9 and p10.
The k = 2 local optimum from lesson 2, inertia 30.4167. It is worse by the objective, yet it puts all five of cause 1 together and only misplaces p10.
k-means k = 3 at its optimum, inertia 10.8. p10 now gets its own cluster, matching cause 3 exactly, but p9 is still with cause 2's points.
DBSCAN, eps = 1.5, minPts = 3. Both clusters are pure, and the two points it could not place, p9 and p10, are exactly the two the truth treats as awkward.

blocks.md: The **Rand index** counts pairs of points: of all $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs, what fraction do the two partitions agree about, either putting both together or both apart? Its problem is that it does not sit at 0 for a random answer. The **adjusted Rand index** subtracts the agreement you would expect by chance, from the row and column totals of the contingency table.

blocks.caption: n_ij is the count in cell (i,j), a_i the row totals and b_j the column totals. The scikit-learn range is -0.5 to 1, with 1 for identical partitions and about 0 for random labelling at any n and any number of clusters.

blocks.md:
Worked on the first scene, k-means k = 2 at its optimum. The cells are 4, 1, 4 and 1, so $\sum_{ij} \binom{n_{ij}}{2} = 6 + 0 + 6 + 0 = 12$. Row totals 5, 4, 1 give $10 + 6 + 0 = 16$; column totals 4, 6 give $6 + 15 = 21$; and $\binom{10}{2} = 45$.

Expected agreement is $16 \times 21 / 45 = 7.4667$, so

ARI $= (12 - 7.4667) / (18.5 - 7.4667) = 4.5333 / 11.0333 = 0.4109$.

The plain Rand index for the same table is 0.7111, which sounds much more impressive for the same clustering.

blocks.title: Rand index, ARI and NMI for six candidate clusterings

scenes.caption: Unadjusted Rand index. Ten singleton clusters score 0.6444 and the one-cluster answer 0.3556, so the scale has no fixed meaning: 0.64 here is pure chance.
ARI. Both degenerate answers now score exactly 0.0, as the chance correction intends, and DBSCAN with its two noise labels scores 0.7469.
NMI. The one-cluster answer is 0.0, but ten singletons score 0.5812: unadjusted mutual information rises as you add clusters, so NMI rewards over-splitting.

blocks.md: Look at the first two bars. The k = 2 clustering with the *better* inertia, 28.8333, scores ARI 0.4109, while the local optimum with the worse inertia, 30.4167, scores 0.7734. Optimising the objective harder moved the answer away from the truth. Inertia is a proxy, and this is what it means for a proxy to be imperfect: never argue from inertia to correctness.

The noise column hides a second trap. DBSCAN at eps = 1.5 scores ARI 0.7469 when you treat -1 as one more label. If instead you drop the two noise points and score only the eight it clustered, both clusters are perfectly pure and ARI is **1.0000**. Both numbers are defensible, and only one of them is honest on its own: a method can buy a perfect score by abstaining on anything hard. Report the pair, the score and the coverage, or score noise as its own cluster and say so.

Metric caveats, straight from the user guide. ARI and the mutual information scores "require the knowledge of the ground truth classes", which you almost never have at scale. The unadjusted Rand index "is often close to 1.0 even if the clusterings themselves differ significantly". NMI and MI "are not adjusted against chance" and MI "will tend to increase as the number of different labels increases"; the chance-corrected version is the adjusted mutual information, AMI.

blocks.question: A clustering of 10000 log lines scores Rand index 0.93 and ARI 0.02 against a hand-labelled sample. What happened?
options: The two metrics measure different things, so this is normal and the result is good
The clustering agrees with the labels about as well as a random partition does, and the high Rand index is just the many pairs that any fine-grained split keeps apart
The sample is too small for ARI, which needs at least as many labels as clusters
ARI must be negative to indicate a problem, so 0.02 still means strong agreement
blocks.explain: With many clusters, almost every pair of points is separated in both partitions and counts as agreement, which pushes the raw Rand index up. ARI subtracts that expected agreement, and about 0 means chance level. Trust the chance-corrected number.

blocks.question: Two pipelines are compared on the same 50000 incidents. A clusters everything and scores silhouette 0.31. B marks 60 percent as noise and scores silhouette 0.78 on the rest. Which conclusion is sound?
options: B found much better clusters, since 0.78 is far above 0.31
Neither score means anything without ground truth labels
A is better, because a higher coverage always beats a higher silhouette
The scores are not comparable, because B is scored on a different and much easier subset of points
blocks.explain: Internal metrics are computed on the points you give them. Dropping the 60 percent that are hardest to place inflates any geometry-based score, so B's 0.78 is a statement about 40 percent of the data. Compare them at equal coverage, or score noise as a cluster. Whether 40 percent coverage is acceptable is a product decision, not a metric one, and internal scores are precisely the scores you can compute without labels.

blocks.question: You want one number to track nightly as a clustering pipeline changes, with a small hand-labelled sample available. Which choice best survives a change in the number of clusters the pipeline emits?
options: Unadjusted NMI, since it is bounded by 1
Inertia, since it is what k-means optimises
ARI or AMI, because both are corrected for chance and so do not drift when the number of clusters changes
Mean silhouette, since it needs no labels
blocks.explain: Chance-corrected metrics stay near 0 for random labellings at any number of clusters, so a jump in cluster count does not by itself move them. Unadjusted MI and NMI rise with more clusters, inertia falls with more clusters and is not comparable across different k or different features, and the silhouette also shifts with k and favours compact blobs. Track a chance-corrected external metric plus the coverage.
